### **MARKET DEVELOPMENTS** 

_Official quotes rise sharply during the first half of the month_ 

_Prices remain sensitive to macro economic data releases_ 

_Sentiment dampened by concern over possible slowdown in Chinese demand_ 

Thus far in June, official 3-month LME copper prices averaged $5026/t (to the 29<sup>th</sup> ) up by 10% compared with the May average of $4581/t, the highest monthly average since September 2008.  Despite the overall upward trend there were three distinct phases to movements in prices during the month.  Between the end of May and the 11<sup>th</sup> of June prices rose from $4787/t to an eight-month high of $5290/t.  From the 12<sup>th</sup> to the 23<sup>rd</sup> a sell off ensued which led to the loss of almost all of the gains made up until the 11<sup>th</sup> .  As a consequence, 3-month official quotes fell by $464/t (-8.8%) from the month’s peak of $5290/t on the 11<sup>th</sup> to the month’s low of $4826/t on the 23<sup>rd</sup> .  Since then prices (3m) have recovered and are trading around $5160/t at the time of writing. 

We believe that the price increase during the first phase (the end of May and the 11<sup>th</sup> of June) was driven primarily by the release of positive macro economic data.  In the US, it was reported that the Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) rose for the fifth consecutive month in May.  The most notable contribution was from new orders which rose above 50, the level between expansion and contraction, for the first time in 18 months.  Elsewhere in the US, the number of people claiming unemployment benefit fell for the first time in 17 weeks during the week ending 23<sup>rd</sup> May.  Meanwhile in China, May auto sales surged by 34% year on year.  Chinese fixed asset investment also rose during the first five months of the year, up by 32.9% year on year.  Finally, in Japan industrial production rose by 5.2% in April from a month earlier.  This represented the fastest month-onmonth gain in 56 years.  Furthermore, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI), is forecasting additional monthly increases in May (+8.8%) and June (+2.7%).  In turn, these data releases led to an improvement in sentiment and the establishment of fresh long positions by the fund community.  Evidence of these long positions can be found in the 7.8k lot rise in open interest over the same period as 3-month quotes increased by $503/t. 

The decline in prices that occurred between the 12<sup>th</sup> and the 23<sup>rd</sup> of the month highlights how fickle investors can be given the uncertainty surrounding the evolution of the current recession.  No sooner had the market reacted to positive indicators when uncertainty returned and sentiment was dampened by growing speculation over the pending seasonal slowdown in

Chinese demand, a stronger dollar and renewed concerns about the macro economic outlook. In the latter case, this mainly stemmed from reports that the US capacity utilisation rate fell to a record low of 68.3% in May. ##### **WEEKLY COPPER EXCHANGE STOCKS AND CASH LME PRICE** kt $/tonne

_Page 2_ _June 2009_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ Total exchange stocks declined for the fourth consecutive month in June, falling by a net 16.4kt to 376.3kt through to the 29th . Similar to May, net increases in Comex (+3.7kt) and SHFE (+25.9kt) warehouses were outweighed by a 46kt decline in LME stocks. As of the 29th inventories on Comex, SHFE and the LME totalled 54.3kt, 56.1kt and 266kt respectively. The sharp rise in SHFE inventories, to their highest level since August 2007, was not unexpected as May imports remained at record levels at a time when demand was becoming seasonally slower. However, imports in the coming months are not expected to be as high as May because the SHFE/LME arbitrage has narrowed. Elsewhere, LME inventories declined on a daily basis and are now at their lowest level since November last year. The majority of withdrawals occurred from US locations where stocks declined by a net 30.6kt to 187.3kt. Deliveries from warehouses in New Orleans (-24kt) accounted for the majority of the decline. In Europe, LME inventories declined by a net 15.3kt reaching 76.8kt. Cancelled warrants also declined during the month, falling from 36.7kt at the end of May to 10.6kt as of the 29th , implying that further withdrawals will take place in the coming weeks, albeit at a much reduced level. European premia remained firm during June, reflecting a small improvement in copper semis demand and consumer restocking in preparation for an expected pick up in demand in September following the summer shutdown period in the Northern Hemisphere. As a consequence Chilean and grade A material from Rotterdam continued to trade between $70-90/t. Italian warrants remained at the higher level of $90-100/t, reflecting tight availability. Premia for standard grade material rose from $10-20/t in May to $20-25/t in June as the ongoing tightness in scrap supply continued to provide support. In the US, premia were unchanged at 4.5-5.5c/lb as business slowed ahead of the summer shutdown period. Although there were reports of some last minute orders (ahead of the holiday season) which helped support premia levels. Meanwhile in China, premia softened during June, easing from $150-160/t at the beginning of the month, to around $130/t at the time of writing. The weaker levels ref

lected the SHFE/LME arbitrage turning negative during June. As of the 29th SHFE quotes traded an average $33/t (net of VAT) _below_ LME prices. This compared with an average _premium_ of $146/t in May and $428/t in April. Latest trade data showed that refined imports in May reached a new monthly record of 337.2kt. This was up by 258% (+243kt) from a year earlier on the back of an average SHFE/LME arbitrage of $428/t in April. For the first five months of the year refined copper imports totalled 1.4Mt, an increase of 130% (+792kt) from the corresponding period in 2008. _Chinese scrap imports held up in ports_ _Demand in the mature economies expected to improve in H2_ _Chinese demand expected to moderate in H2_ So far this year China's uptake of metal units has more than compensated for the general malaise in demand within the mature economies. As we turn into the second half of the year there is growing uncertainty as to whether China can continue to absorb metal at the pace that was seen in H1 2009. Scrap imports into China have massively underperformed last year's levels, partly due to higher margins on initial payments compared with cathode (70% compared with 2030%) and lower availability at the start of the year due to very low copper prices in December, a general unwillingness of scrap dealers to sell "expensive" scrap at a loss, as well as a there being a large number of smaller dealers that simply went broke. During the first five months of this year Chinese scrap imports declined by almost 40%, year on year, including a 34% annual decline in May. The current issue with scrap is not so much a lack of supply, but the renewed desire by the Chinese authorities to clamp down on illegal and misclassified imports that have been occurring in order to avoid or reduce tax payments. Heightened inspection activities have caused a massive backlog of containers in southern Chinese ports which means that there is now a large logistical bottleneck. Latest reports suggest that the number of containers currently sat in ports in southern China is estimated at 6k (although this bottleneck is now starting to ease). While this is positive for cathode consumption, it is difficult to gauge how long th

is will remain so.  Another uncertainty surrounds the robustness of Chinese consumption growth in H2.  Some of the seasonal positives have now passed (Q1 restocking, peak demand for air conditioner production etc.) although demand from the power sector should remain strong over the balance of the year. 

At the same time, there is a huge amount of uncertainty surrounding whether there will be any recovery within the mature economies.  The dramatic decline in copper consumption in Q1 (y-o-y) was in part a reflection of destocking.  Is this phase now over and does this mean that even a moderate pick up in end use demand will have a more positive effect on first use cathode consumption? German copper producer, Aurubis, recently reported an improvement in demand for its copper and copper alloy products.  This begs the question as to whether the upturn is localised or more regionally based.  Our sources indicate that European demand has improved but the picture is somewhat mixed.  One European wire rod producer mainly supplying the high tension market reported reasonable order levels and as a result output is at 85/90% of “budgeted production levels”.  Meanwhile wire producers supplying the automotive sector are operating at only 60% of budgeted production targets although order levels going forward are looking more promising, especially for July and August, traditionally slow months (See Consumption).  Likewise in the US, there are signs of improvement but these are mixed.  Wire rod producers continue to suffer from the weak wire and cable sector while copper semis producers have seen a pick up in demand from the electrical and electronic industries (See consumption). 

Taking the above into account our base case assumption is that Chinese refined consumption growth will moderate somewhat in H2 on the back of improving scrap supplies while higher metal prices may encourage consumers to hold less stock.  Also, the SRB is unlikely to be active in H2 2009 given the increase in prices which will make copper a far less attractive investment moving forward. We forecast that the mature economies and countries outside of China will experience less negative consumption growth during H2 2009 which, together with an end to the destocking that was so apparent in H1, will help offset the

slowing pace of Chinese refined consumption with the result that any global stock build is likely to be modest.  With the moderate stock build in absolute terms and with stocks in days of consumption forecast to remain flat at around 60 days we expect prices to average $4300/t ($1.95/lb) in H2, or 25% above the Q1 level and 8% below Q2.  For 2009 as a whole we forecast that cash prices will average $4179/t ($1.90/lb). 

Looking further forward into 2010 we expect that the copper market will, for the fourth consecutive year, record a surplus in absolute terms.  Whilst refined consumption is forecast to increase by

2.5%, supply should outstrip demand with the result that we are forecasting a global market surplus of just over 250kt taking stocks to 67 days of consumption, up slightly on 2009. With metal inventories continuing to increase, quarter on quarter, throughout the year, despite the start of a recovery in developed world demand, this is likely to weigh on market sentiment and prices. Our average price for the 2010 is $3975/t ($1.80/lb), the lowest average price in nominal terms since 2005. 2011 will mark the start of a meaningful recovery in the fortunes of the copper market. Refined consumption is forecast to rise by 6.1% reflecting synchronised global growth together with significant inventory adjustments (restocking). Refined production on the other hand is forecast to rise by just 3%. The overall effect of these changes is that stock levels are expected to be reduced to 58 days of consumption. As a result, LME cash prices are forecast to be on a rising trend throughout the year, averaging $4625/t ($2.10/lb). _Surplus forecast for 2010, for the fourth consecutive year…_ _.. but the market’s fortunes are expected to improve in 2011_ **PRICE FORECASTS AND WORLD QUARTERLY SUPPLY/DEMAND BALANCE – (kt)** ||**Refined**

_Page 6_ _June 2009_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ ### **ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS** There have been some modest improvements in leading economic indicators over the past month, particularly in China and India, pointing to a slowdown in the rate of contraction in global industrial output during the second half of 2009. However, we have serious doubts about the robustness of these green shoots of recovery, and still do not anticipate sustained growth in output for most major economies until mid-2010. In the USA, new orders for manufactured durable goods rose by 1.8% in May from April, despite some heavy falls in vehicle orders, marking the second consecutive monthly gain. Although the increase in orders is encouraging for an increase in manufacturing in the coming months, the fact that shipments of durable goods continued to fall in May, down by a further 2.1% from April, highlights that demand is still extremely weak. Industrial production continued to slide in May, falling 1.1% from April and 13.4% from May 2008 to its lowest level since 1998. Capacity utilization the US industrial sector was just 68.3% in May, the lowest number on records going back to 1967. With much of the woes of the US economic downturn stemming from the collapse of its housing market, the apparent stabilisation of US housing construction is being taken as an encouraging sign. Housing starts in May rose by 17.2% from April, although were still down by 45.2% from May 2008, and sales of existing homes increased by 2.4% month on month in May. However, the main area for concern is the housing stock. The stock of unoccupied houses has barely fallen from its peaks at the end of 2007, while home sales have fallen dramatically. On top of this, the number of foreclosures each month continues to grow. In May, the number of existi

ng properties for sale stood at 9.6 months of supply, based on current sales rates.  This overhang of stock needs to be cleared, something that is likely to take several quarters, before prices firm and construction activity stages a significant recovery. 

China’s domestic stimulus package appears to be keeping its economy growing while the global economy languishes.  Fixed asset investment in May increased by 38.7% from a year earlier, and for the year to date it has grown by 32.9% from the first five months of 2008, with much of the investment increase accounted for by state directed projects.  China’s monetary stimulus too appears to have been effective, with total bank lending in May growing by 30.6% year on year, slightly above the growth rate in recent months and much stronger than the ~15% growth rate seen through much of 2008. 

Industrial output in China increased by a robust 8.9% year on year in May; the strongest growth since September 2008, but still significantly below the extremely vigorous growth rates seen in previous years.  The figure was boosted by a 35% rise in vehicle production, driven by rising passenger vehicle sales, which grew by a massive 47% year on year in May, and are up annually by 14% for the first five months of 2009.  The primary concern for China’s economy remains the weakness overseas. Exports in May tumbled by a record 26.4% from May 2008, with demand from the US, Europe, Japan and Korea sluggish. 

We have made downward revisions to our global industrial output forecasts.  We now estimate that global IP will fall by 7.6% in 2009, and grow by just 1.7% in 2010.  The revision is mainly a result of downgrading our expectations for the OECD countries, where we anticipate a contraction in IP of 11.4% in 2009 and 0.4% in 2010.  In China, we have upgraded our China IP growth forecasts to an average of 7.9% in 2009 and 2010, based upon the improvement in output growth, but are concerned about the lack of demand for finished goods from China’s major export destinations.

### **CONSUMPTION** 

_Downturn in demand exacerbated by destocking…_ 

_.. thus global demand forecast to decline by 3.5% this year_ 

_Flailing export demand continues to plague European demand for copper_ 

_European construction activity forecast to decline in 2009_ 

The collapse in economic activity, which began in Q3 last year, has been exacerbated by savage destocking at all levels of the global consumption chain. This, in turn, has continued to have a dramatic impact on global copper demand (ex China) throughout Q2.  However, the destocking proce

ss is now showing tentative signs to suggest that it may be coming to an end, with inventories now more closely aligned to demand. In some cases there have been some indications of restocking. However, with end-user demand still at extremely low levels restocking will be minimal. Many consumers are adjusting inventories on a week-to-week basis to ensure that they have material to meet their work-inhand needs. Taking the above into account we forecast that global refined copper consumption will decrease by 3.5% this year to ~17.3Mt. This is down from our previous estimate of -3.2% growth and largely reflects downward revisions made to our Japanese figures where the downturn in demand thus far this year has been much sharper than we previously anticipated. In 2010 we forecast that demand will recover moderately, increasing by 2.5% to 17.7Mt,. However, it is not until 2011 that we project that global refined copper consumption will rise sharply, increasing by 6.1% to just under 18.8Mt. This will reflect the combination of restocking, pent up consumer and business demand and the full effects of the various infrastructure-related stimulus measures that have been introduced so far this year. European economies continue to suffer form falling export demand for the region’s manufactured goods as well weak activity within the auto and construction sectors. According to the Automobile Manufacturers Association European car sales fell by 4.9% year on year in May. This represented the 13th consecutive month of decline on an annual basis. Sales for the first five months of the year totalled 5.8M units, a year on year decline of 14.7%. Meanwhile, European car production totalled 4.7M units, down 27% from the corresponding period in 2008. With total construction output falling by 3.1% in 2008, output in 2009 is expected to decline by 7.5% and by 1% in 2010. Unusually, the contraction is forecast to affect all of the main construction sectors including civil engineering. However, in 2011 the sector as a whole is expected to return to growth. Unsurprisingly the contraction in manufacturing and construction activity has had a devastating impact on the region’s demand for copper and copper alloy products. This is particularly true in Italy where Assomet, Italy’s non-ferrous metal industry body, reported a 28.7% (-97.4kt) year on year decline in the output of copper

and copper alloy products during Q1. The production of copper products declined by 19.2% while copper alloy products fell by 38.1% from a year earlier. Demand for copper wire was particularly weak, where output fell annually by 19.5% through to March. This partly reflected a sharp decline in orders for automotive wire where Italian auto production declined by 38.5% during Q1 from a year ago. Demand for automotive wire has not performed well elsewhere across the region. One wire producer in Germany reported that his production year-to-date is the equivalent of only 60% of his budgeted target. However, on a slightly brighter note, the same producer did report that since May there has been an improvement in demand where order levels for July and August are quite healthy. This mainly reflects restocking within the auto sector where inventories have been run down to very low levels. Also on a positive note, some wire rod producers who supply the power sector reported to us that they have not witnessed a significant drop in orders. Indeed one major German wire rod producer, who supplies the high tension power cable market, is currently producing between 85-90% of his budgeted production target. Meanwhile other wire rod producers are reported to be producing around 70% of their budgeted production level. While there are growing signs to suggest that the decline in European demand for copper may have bottomed, the extent of the downturn in both the region’s auto and construction sectors has been extremely severe so far this year. Thus we continue to forecast a 10% contraction in European refined copper consumption this year to just under 3.1Mt. _June 2009_ _Page 9_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ _No recovery in US copper demand expected any time soon_ _US vehicle production down 52%year on year through to May_ _US construction sector still very volatile_ _US demand for copper wire rod extremely weak_ In the US industrial production, auto production and construction activity has continued to decline. And although some key indicators show signs of the first green shoots of recovery in US economic activity, there is little to suggest that the sustained decline in US copper demand, which began in early 2008, will c

ome to an end any time soon. The decline in US economic activity and subsequence collapse in consumer spending has perhaps been most notable in the auto industry, where two of the big three US carmakers filed for bankruptcy protection during Q2. According to latest government statistics, US vehicle production declined by 52% during the first five months of 2009 from a year earlier. Production schedules released in early June point to a significant pick-up in auto assemblies in the next quarter, although whether these schedules are overly optimistic remains to be seen. Elsewhere in the construction sector, residential construction appears to have established a bottom, although the large excess of housing stock available means a solid rebound in activity is highly unlikely. According to latest government statistics, housing starts in May climbed 17.2% from the record low in April, and are now above the Q1 average of 528k units. However, one month does not a recovery make, and the May figure remains 45% down from May last year and 77% down from the peak of activity at the start of 2006. In addition, the number of foreclosures in the US continues to surge, widening the already substantial gap between housing supply and demand. If foreclosures continue to add significant numbers of houses to the market, prices will come under greater pressure and a recovery in homebuilding activity will be pushed back further. The depressed level of activity in the auto and construction sectors has continued to impact upon US demand for copper. Data released by the American Bureau of Statistics (ABMS) highlighted just how bad US copper consumption has become in 2009. Production of copper wire rod declined by 19.2% year on year in May, marking the 15th consecutive month in which output fell on an annual basis. For the five months of the year as whole, wire rod output plunged 25.5% (-173kt) from the corresponding period in 2008. _Chinese concentrate imports rise (+6.7%) during the first 5 months of 2009_ 

_Xiangguang Copper embarks upon a doubling of its smelter/refinery capacity_ 

_Concentrate supplies, expressed as a percentage of primary smelter capacity, decline from 93% to less than 77% over the past 5 years_ 

According to China’s custom trade statistics the country’s May copper concentrate imports increased by 22.6%, year on year, to 508.9kt.  On a cumulative basis the figure for the first five months was 2.44Mdmt which represented an uplift of 6.7% on the same period in 2008.  Imports from Peru have increased by 21% year on year thus far in 2009 pushing Chile (-38.7%) into second place in terms of tonnage received.  Deliveries from Iran (99kt) were substantially higher compared with 2008 (+332%) and with Iranian shipments to India expected to more than double this year, (i.e. to 220kt) this would tend to substantiate recent rumours that this middle eastern producer had accumulated large stocks of concentrates over the past year or so. 

Last month we noted the emergence of a further three Chinese copper smelter projects, these having a combined incremental capacity of in excess of 200kt/a. This trend has continued through June with the announcement by Xiangguang Copper that it had embarked upon an expansion to double the size of its smelter, from 200kt/a to 400kt/a with completion anticipated in H2 2010.  Last year the complex produced 106kt of refined copper and this year’s total is likely to be in the range of 160 to 165kt Cu. 

The growth in China’s primary copper smelting capacity in recent years has occurred at a time when there have been substantial disruptions to copper-inconcentrate output.  Over the period 1996 to 2005 copper-in-concentrate supplies, measured as a percent of primary smelting capacity, peaked at 93% and averaged 88% (see chart below).  At this level of supply, smelters were able to maintain adequate levels of concentrate stocks and the market was reasonably well balanced.  More recently, supply disruptions have escalated as has the growth in Chinese smelter capacity.  Copper-in-concentrate supplies, net of disruptions, currently equate to less than 77% of primary smelter capacity, which in absolute tonnage terms is equivalent to a shortfall of almost 1.9Mt of copper-in-concentrates relative to the historic optimal utilisation rate of 88%. Worse still, there is seemingly no respite for the smelting industry.  Current indications suggest moving forward into 2010 and 2011 mine supplies will remain below 77% of primary smelting capacity and that the tonnage shortfall relative to optimal levels will remain at around 2Mt of copper-in-concentrates.

_Ultimately, smelter capacity will need to shut down if the concentrate market is to readjust to more sustainable levels for smelters_ Under the scenario mentioned above it is difficult to envisage why TC/RCs will remain anything but depressed with too much smelting capacity chasing too little mine output. China is unlikely to stop adding to its custom smelting capacity given the ongoing shortfall in domestically produced refined copper relative to the country’s demand. Market conditions will ultimately force a correction upon the smelting industry and not necessarily just within the pure _Page 14_ _June 2009_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ custom sector. Hudbay Minerals has recently announced that it expects to close its 90kt/a Flin Flon copper smelter by July 2010. The company’s local mines historically provided 60% of the smelter’s feed with the balance sourced from the custom market. Depressed TC/RCs forced Hudbay to stop purchasing third party concentrates during 2008, impacting on anode output. Low production, high costs and tightening environmental regulations are believed to have been the catalysts for the company’s closure announcement. Ultimately, more smelter closures must follow if the concentrate market is to readjust to more sustainable levels. _Zambian copper producers experience power loss – production losses reportedly negligible_

Another mine that has been experiencing mill problems is PanAust’s Phu Kham operation in Laos.  The failure of a mill motor means that the processing plant is likely to be closed for between 11 to 23 days for the loss of between 2kt to 4kt of copper-in-concentrates.  The company has declared _force majeure_ on concentrate shipments. 

Power supplies to Zambia’s copper operations have been disrupted on several occasions during the past four weeks.  At the start of the month it was reported that a water weed had choked the flow of water into a dam at the Kafue Gorge power station forcing the state-owned power utility, Zesco, to halt some of its generating units.  Subsequently in mid month, power was again disrupted following a transformer fire at the Leopards Hill substation.  The effect on most copper operations was fairly minimal because additional power was quickly sourced from neighbouring DRC stations.   According to the Bank of Zambia, during the first four months of 2009 the country’s copper output increased by almost 14%, year on year to 218.1kt due in part to the contribution from the new 170kt/a Lumwana mine. 

It seems that China will not change a $9Bn investment accord with the DRC despite the IMF threatening to withhold $10Bn in debt relief and $500M in financial support from the DRC unless it is altered.  The IMF is unhappy because the accord effectively adds to the DRC’s national debt due to the country being the guarantor of the entire debt if the deal falters.  The deal, which was signed in 2008 between China’s Exim Bank, the Kinshasa Government, Gecamines, China Railway Engineering Corp. and Sinohydro Corp. provides for the Chinese side to invest $6Bn in infrastructure projects within the DRC and a further $3Bn in mine development.  Various DRC ore deposits containing 10Mt of Cu and 600kt of Co, including Dikuluwe and Mashamba West, are to be developed and/or rehabilitated with the Chinese owning 68% of the venture and Gecamines the remainder.  The DRC is to pay back the $9Bn loan from its share of the mines’ profits.
